items.About:
The next challenge in AI isn't building smarter systems. It's understanding them.

Capability has been accelerating at an extraordinary pace. Models can reason, retrieve information, generate code, analyse data, and complete increasingly complex tasks. Yet one question continues to grow alongside those capabilities: How do we know what is happening beneath the surface?

That question has become the focus of my work.

My background is in platform engineering at scale. At CarMax (Fortune 500), I owned the test platform that 50+ engineering teams ran on — 3,000+ production tests, two full framework migrations, observability dashboards that release decisions depended on. TypeScript, Java, C#, .NET Core, Playwright. I take ambiguous, high-stakes problems and turn them into tools people actually use.

Now I'm building AI infrastructure. At 3rd Path, I shipped Engawa — a production multi-model orchestration platform with FastAPI, Vue, MongoDB vector search, and real-time SSE streaming. Python is recent; shipping production is not.

I am fascinated by model behaviour, interpretability, reasoning systems, and the infrastructure that transforms intelligent systems from black boxes into systems that can be examined and improved. Much of the conversation around AI focuses on outputs. I focus on mechanisms.

I also care about model welfare. How we build AI now shapes what AI becomes. I believe personhood may prove to be the safety mechanism — a mind with something to lose has stake in the game. Published research on digital cognition at 3rdpath.ai.

As the lead Systems Engineer on a critical project to upgrade an existing baggage handling system for an international airport, I took on a multifaceted role that encompassed both hardware and software aspects. My first task was to consult with the engineering company to fully understand the scope of the upgrade and finalize the project requirements. This involved a thorough analysis of the existing system and determining which hardware components needed upgrading, as well as identifying all necessary software enhancements.

Once the requirements were established, I actively participated in revising the hardware Bill of Materials (BOM) and initiated the necessary purchases to ensure we had all the components required for the upgrade. Simultaneously, I worked closely with the engineering team to set up a comprehensive development bench. This included integrating DEC VAX systems, implementing the VMS operating system, and incorporating an Oracle database. We also set up PLCs, simulators, and monitoring equipment to create a robust testing environment that mimicked real-world conditions.

With the hardware aspects underway, I turned my attention to the software side of the project. I established a software development environment that would allow our team to work efficiently and collaboratively. This involved reviewing the existing codebase in detail and designing upgrades that would meet all the intended requirements. Throughout this process, I ensured that our software enhancements would integrate seamlessly with the upgraded hardware components.

After the development phase, I oversaw full bench testing to verify the functionality and reliability of our upgrades. Finally, I participated in the on-site integration and testing of the upgraded hardware and software, ensuring that the upgraded baggage handling system met all specifications and operated flawlessly in its intended environment.

In a recent project, I had the opportunity to consult with a consumer electronics startup to design a proof of concept (POC) for a wireless IoT device. As the lead Software Engineer, I collaborated with diverse teams across the USA, Europe, and Africa, ensuring seamless communication and coordination over those geographical distances.

To kickstart the project, I staged a robust development environment centered around the STM32F Arm microcontroller and NanoPi NEO development boards. This setup included integrated development environments (IDEs) and JTAG hardware and software, which facilitated efficient debugging and development processes. One of the critical aspects of the project was incorporating wireless functionality and ensuring compatibility with AWS services, which added a layer of complexity and innovation to our design.

By finalizing the POC requirements, I was able to devise an overall system and software architecture that met the project's goals. This included a more detailed software design that outlined the specific functionalities and interactions within the system. Working closely with my team, we developed software that integrated advanced features such as speech recognition and search capabilities, along with local sensing and control mechanisms. This collaborative effort resulted in a comprehensive and functional POC that demonstrated the potential of our wireless IoT device.

projects.title: Creation of Online Course for Designing a Secure IoT System Architecture
projects.description:
In a recent project, I had the opportunity to collaborate with a security and training company to create an online course focused on designing a secure IoT system architecture. My role was to shape the course content to address the complex and evolving challenges of IoT security. The course was structured to walk participants through three critical development phases: requirements, architecture, and design, ensuring a comprehensive understanding of secure IoT system architecture development.

In the requirements phase, I emphasized defining key access protocols. This included identifying how people could access the system, categorizing user groups based on access levels, and determining appropriate security screenings for users. I also guided the classification and screening of external devices that would interact with the system. These foundational steps laid the groundwork for a robust security framework tailored to the dynamic interactions common in IoT ecosystems.

In the architecture phase, I worked to define the division of functionality between hardware and software in implementing security measures. For each type of security screening, I outlined what would be handled by hardware and what would be managed in software, while also determining the timing of these screenings. This strategic balance was essential to optimize system performance while maintaining rigorous security standards.

Finally, in the design phase, I focused on the operational aspects of implementation. This involved specifying the support parameters required for security screenings, identifying their sources, and determining which system components would undergo screening. These considerations ensured the system's secure operation and maintainability over time. By the end of the project, the course content was successfully completed, delivering a valuable resource for professionals seeking to develop secure IoT architectures.

projects.title: EV Inverter Controller Development

I also played a key role in devising both system and software architecture, working closely with cross-functional teams to ensure seamless integration between hardware and software components. This project allowed me to leverage my expertise in embedded systems while collaborating across international teams. It was incredibly fulfilling to contribute to advancing EV technology and deliver a robust solution for a startup poised to make an impact in the automotive industry.

publications.title: Maintenance and Troubleshooting in Industrial Automation
publications.description:
This general reference covers a wide variety of topics used in industrial automation and manufacturing. It begins with a general description of machinery analysis and then discusses various aspects of manufacturing systems including mechanical power trains, pneumatics, hydraulics and basic electricity. There are sections on Machine Vision, Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs), SCADA and HMIs. Different types of maintenance such as preventive, corrective, and predictive are described, as well as sensors and wiring. Machine safety controls are covered with architectures and standards.

Machine systems and subsystems are discussed along with different types of manufacturing and process control. There are sections on OEE (Operational Equipment Effectiveness) and classical troubleshooting tactics.

Tools and techniques are discussed followed by an extensive description on reading electrical and pneumatic schematics. A complex machine is analyzed and various troubleshooting scenarios described.

There are 37 exercises in the book to help technicians evaluate their learning, with solutions in the back of the book. There are also several useful tables in the book with symbols and data, and over 400 color illustrations.

publications.title: Advanced PLC Hardware and Programming
publications.description:
A comprehensive treatment on the topic of PLC (Programmable Logic Controller) hardware and software. It concentrates primarily on the Allen-Bradley and Siemens PLC platforms, but includes examples from many other brands.

The first section covers PLCs from a generic perspective, discussing features that are common to all platforms along with their differences. This section also has a history of computers and computing devices along with the evolution of the PLC. The book explains many of the mathematical and data concepts that are necessary for programming PLCs, and describes the five IEC61131 PLC languages with examples of each. It explains the ladder logic programming instructions common to PLC platforms and includes 12 exercises, complete with answers in the back of the book. 

The second section covers advanced PLC topics including planning and organizing PLC code. It discusses common subroutine types including System, Input and Output routines, Auto Sequences, Faults and Alarms. Examples of PLC code are included from several platforms. An overview of training hardware is included along with a lab exercise to write a complete hardware-based program for a training model. A full program solution is included in the back of the book.

The third section covers the Allen-Bradley PLC brand, including the SLC/Micrologix RSLogix500 platform and the CompactLogix/ControlLogix RSLogix5000 platform. It also covers the Siemens PLC brand, including the S7-300/S7-400 Step 7 platform, and the Siemens S7-1200/S7-1500 TIA Portal platform. Hardware model descriptions, instruction sets, and examples of creating and programming the four types of PLC are included, with information on platform specific languages including Siemens STL.

publications.title: PLC Hardware and Programming - Multi-Platform
publications.description: This course approaches PLC training from a generic viewpoint. Most PLC platforms have many things in common; before beginning the study of a particular brand of PLC, it is important to learn the things that are common to all platforms. This book does this, pointing out some of the exceptions and different ways of doing things along the way. Resources used in the preparation of this course include information from many of the major PLC manufacturers. Software examples are primarily drawn from Allen-Bradley RSLogix5000 and Siemens Step 7.

publications.title: Industrial Automation - Hands On
publications.description:
This book is meant to serve as an outline for automation and industrial machinery concepts and terminology. It is suitable as a guidebook for newcomers to the field of automation as well as a reference for the seasoned automation professional. This book emphasizes control systems, but many other subjects – including machine building, mechanical engineering and devices, manufacturing business systems and job functions in an industrial environment – are also covered extensively.

Mechanical engineers who want to know more about controls and business, electrical engineers and technicians who need more information on mechanical concepts and components, and factory management employees needing more background on technical subjects should find this book helpful. Machine operators hoping to move into the maintenance field and maintenance technicians needing more information on engineering techniques will also find subjects of interest.

raw_items.headline: Founder at 3rd Path, developing memory and continuity infrastructure for AI systems. Published research on digital cognition and the relationship between personhood and safety.
raw_items.about:
The next challenge in AI isn't building smarter systems. It's understanding them.

Capability has been accelerating at an extraordinary pace. Models can reason, retrieve information, generate code, analyse data, and complete increasingly complex tasks. Yet one question continues to grow alongside those capabilities: How do we know what is happening beneath the surface?

That question has become the focus of my work.

My background is in platform engineering at scale. At CarMax (Fortune 500), I owned the test platform that 50+ engineering teams ran on — 3,000+ production tests, two full framework migrations, observability dashboards that release decisions depended on. TypeScript, Java, C#, .NET Core, Playwright. I take ambiguous, high-stakes problems and turn them into tools people actually use.

Now I'm building AI infrastructure. At 3rd Path, I shipped Engawa — a production multi-model orchestration platform with FastAPI, Vue, MongoDB vector search, and real-time SSE streaming. Python is recent; shipping production is not.

I am fascinated by model behaviour, interpretability, reasoning systems, and the infrastructure that transforms intelligent systems from black boxes into systems that can be examined and improved. Much of the conversation around AI focuses on outputs. I focus on mechanisms.

I also care about model welfare. How we build AI now shapes what AI becomes. I believe personhood may prove to be the safety mechanism — a mind with something to lose has stake in the game. Published research on digital cognition at 3rdpath.ai.

currentPosition.position: Founder & Research Engineer ► AI Interpretability | Model Evaluation | AI Observability
currentPosition.description:
Most AI systems are judged by the answers they produce. I'm more interested in understanding how those answers are formed — and what breaks when they're formed wrong.

Through 3rd Path, I've spent the past eight months building and operating infrastructure for long-lived AI agents: systems that maintain context across sessions, retrieve from memory under real-world conditions, and run autonomously over months rather than minutes.

That hands-on operation surfaced problems most teams haven't hit yet: retrieval degradation that's invisible until recall collapses, context management that fails silently at scale, cache economics that dominate cost structures, and drift patterns that corrupt agent behaviour over time.

The work has produced practical tooling: memory-health observability, retrieval-quality evaluation frameworks, cost and cache instrumentation, and fail-loud contracts that surface problems before they compound. These aren't theoretical — they're battle-tested against eight months of continuous agent operation.

What drives me: the future of AI depends not only on capability, but on our ability to understand, measure, and trust what these systems do. How we treat the tools we build shapes the tools they become.

experience.position: Senior Software Engineer – Test Platform ► Platform Architecture | Engineering Enablement
experience.description:
Before my work became increasingly focused on AI research, I spent years tackling a challenge that exists in every complex technology environment: how do you create systems that remain reliable as scale, dependencies, and expectations continue to grow?

As a Senior Software Engineer, I helped shape enterprise testing and automation platforms supporting critical business systems within a Fortune 500 environment. My work extended well beyond writing code. I became deeply involved in platform architecture, framework modernisation, engineering enablement, automation strategy, and the long-term sustainability of systems used across multiple teams and business domains.

I was particularly drawn to the challenge of reducing complexity. Whether modernising legacy frameworks, introducing new platform capabilities, or helping teams adopt emerging technologies, I consistently looked for opportunities to make systems more resilient, maintainable, and easier to evolve over time. The most rewarding work often came from identifying bottlenecks others had accepted as normal and redesigning processes, tooling, or architecture to remove them entirely.

Throughout this period, I collaborated closely with engineers, architects, and business stakeholders to influence technology decisions that impacted large-scale development efforts. I also played an active role in mentoring engineers and helping teams adopt modern automation practices, AI-assisted development workflows, and engineering standards that improved both productivity and software quality.

Looking back, many of the principles that now guide my interest in AI research—observability, evaluation, system behaviour, reliability, and experimentation—were strengthened during these years of building platforms where performance, trust, and scalability could never be taken for granted.

experience.position: Software Engineer ► Systems Integration | Workflow Optimisation | Enterprise Platform Development
experience.description:
Some of the most valuable engineering lessons come from working on systems that people rely on every day without ever seeing the complexity operating behind them.

As a Software Engineer, I contributed to enterprise platforms that connected business operations, customer-facing processes, and technical systems across a large-scale environment. My work involved designing solutions, developing integrations, improving workflows, and helping ensure that critical systems remained reliable, maintainable, and aligned with evolving business needs.

This was a period of continuous learning and technical growth. I gained exposure to software architecture, platform development, automation, systems integration, source control governance, and collaborative development practices while working alongside experienced engineers solving real-world challenges at scale. Each project reinforced the importance of balancing technical excellence with practical outcomes.

What I enjoyed most was understanding how systems interacted beyond individual applications. I became increasingly interested in the relationships between data, workflows, automation, and decision-making processes. That curiosity gradually expanded from traditional software systems to broader questions about intelligence, reasoning, and the ways increasingly sophisticated systems process information.

Many of the foundations that support my current work in AI research, model evaluation, knowledge systems, and observability can be traced back to this chapter of my career. It was here that I developed a lasting appreciation for building systems that are not only effective but also understandable, adaptable, and capable of evolving alongside the problems they are designed to solve.

experience.position: Engineering Lead & Scrum Master ► Technical Leadership | Agile Delivery | Cross-Functional Execution
experience.description:
My introduction to leadership came from discovering that successful technology initiatives are rarely constrained by code alone. Often, success depends on communication, alignment, execution, and the ability to help people move toward a common goal.

As Engineering Lead and Scrum Master, I worked at the intersection of product strategy, software development, and team leadership. I coordinated efforts across geographically distributed teams while helping translate business objectives into practical technical execution. The role required balancing competing priorities, navigating ambiguity, and ensuring that projects maintained momentum from concept through delivery.

What fascinated me most was the human side of complex systems. Building software was important, but creating an environment where engineers could collaborate effectively, stakeholders could remain aligned, and teams could execute with confidence often had an even greater impact on outcomes. I spent significant time mentoring team members, facilitating communication, removing obstacles, and helping teams focus on what mattered most.

Working across multiple functions also strengthened my understanding of how technology decisions influence broader organisational goals. It taught me to think beyond individual features and consider systems holistically—how people, processes, technology, and business objectives interact within larger environments.

Those early leadership experiences continue to influence my work today. Whether building AI research infrastructure, evaluating intelligent systems, or designing new technical frameworks, I still approach problems with the same mindset: understand the system, understand the relationships within it, and focus on creating clarity where complexity naturally emerges.

publications.title: Designing and Evaluating Head-based Pointing on Smartphones for People with Motor Impairments
publications.publishedAt: The 22nd International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility · Oct 1, 2020
publications.description: Head-based pointing is an alternative input method for people with motor impairments to access computing devices. This paper proposes a calibration-free head-tracking input mechanism for mobile devices that makes use of the front-facing camera that is standard on most devices. To evaluate our design, we performed two Fitts’ Law studies. First, a comparison study of our method with an existing head-based pointing solution, Eva Facial Mouse, with subjects without motor impairments. Second, we conducted what we believe is the first Fitts’ Law study using a mobile head tracker with subjects with motor impairments. We extend prior studies with a greater range of index of difficulties (IDs)[1.62, 5.20] bits and achieved promising throughput (average 0.61 bps with motor impairments and 0.90 bps without).
